summary: This RFC describes the Resource Location Protocol, which lets a host ask on its network where a service or resource can be found. It works best on networks that support broadcast, but can be used elsewhere. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
Sometimes a host needs to find a service without knowing any address: a gateway to the rest of the Internet, or a name server.

This RFC lets a host broadcast that question to its local network. Each host that hears it checks the question against its own list of services and replies with what it provides.

questions: what is the resource location protocol
how do hosts find network services by broadcast
how does rlp resource location work
how does rlp name a resource
what is the local-only flag in rlp
subtitle: A broadcast request that asks the network which host provides a given service.

tldr.problem: A host sometimes needs to find out where a service is provided, such as a gateway to the rest of the Internet or a name server, without knowing any address in advance.
tldr.mechanism: The querying host sends a UDP request naming the resources it wants, either to one host or broadcast to the local network. Each receiving host decomposes the resource name against its own tables and replies with the resources it provides.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies a draft standard for the ARPA Internet community. The protocol is marked Experimental and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 887 is an Experimental document from December 1983 and has not been obsoleted. It describes itself as a draft standard for the ARPA Internet community, and its Appendix A assigns the Resource Location Protocol the well-known UDP port number 39.

sections.title: The Problem RLP Solves
sections.content:
From time to time, Internet hosts face the problem of determining where on the Internet a particular network service or resource is provided. The situation arises when a host needs to send a packet destined for some external network to a gateway on its directly connected network and knows of no gateways, or when a host needs to translate a domain name to an Internet address and knows of no name servers it can ask.

In almost all cases the resource location problem reduces to finding the IP address of some one host, usually any host, either on the directly connected network or elsewhere on the Internet, that understands a given protocol. Most frequently the querying host itself understands that protocol, and it intends to use the protocol with the host it locates, for example to ask a name server for a name-to-address translation. Less frequently the querying host does not understand the protocol itself, and is simply trying to find some other host that does, such as a gateway to forward a packet that cannot be delivered locally.

The protocol is most useful on networks that support broadcast addressing, but it can be used on other kinds of network. The RFC says that for maximum benefit, all hosts which provide significant resources or services to other hosts on the Internet should implement it, and that hosts failing to implement it risk being ignored by other hosts trying to locate resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Some problems are not about sending data but about finding out who to send it to. This RFC is a way to ask the local network that question.

sections.title: How a Resource Is Named
sections.content:
Locating only a particular lowest-level Internet protocol, one that has an assigned protocol number for transport using IP, is not completely sufficient. Many significant services are provided through higher-level protocols that merely use the lower-level ones for transport: FTP, for example, uses TCP for its transport, and this nesting of protocols can be carried out to arbitrary levels.

RLP therefore names a resource by the protocol number assigned to its lowest-level Internet transport protocol and by a variable-length protocol or resource specific identifier. The UDP-based Echo Protocol is named by its protocol number 17 and its 16-bit well-known port number 7. The Internet Control Message Protocol, which has no higher-level client protocols, is named simply by its protocol number 1 and an empty identifier. A protocol that is not yet defined, provided over say TCP, might be named by the protocol number 6, its 16-bit well-known TCP port number, and then some additional fixed or variable-length identifier specific to that port.

In general the components of the identifier are the natural quantities used to demultiplex the protocol at each next higher level.
sections.plainLanguage: A resource name is a list, read left to right. The first part is the IP protocol number, the second is usually a port number, and further parts narrow the service down, such as the file name for a crash dump over TFTP.

sections.title: The Request and Reply Procedure
sections.content:
RLP is a simple request and reply procedure. The querying host constructs a list of the resources it would like to locate and sends a request message on the network. The request may be sent to a particular IP address and host, or, on networks with broadcast address capability, to the IP address that refers to all hosts on that network. A host trying to locate a domain name server, for example, constructs a request containing the resource name [17, 53], referring to the Domain Name Server protocol at well-known UDP port 53, and broadcasts it on its local network.

Each receiving host examines the resource list, determines which of the named resources it provides, and returns a reply to the querying host. It works this out by successive decomposition of the resource name until either the name is exhausted or it meets a component the host does not support. In the domain name server example, each host first checks its tables to see whether it provides UDP service, and then, if it does, checks its UDP table to see whether it provides service on UDP port 53.

There are four request types. <Who-Provides?> asks any host receiving it to reply naming all the resources from the list that it provides, and requires no reply if it provides none. <Do-You-Provide?> is the same but a reply must always be returned, with an empty list if the host provides none, which lets the querying host detect the answer at once instead of waiting for retransmissions. The first is typically used when broadcasting to a whole network; the second is typically used to confirm what one particular host provides, and may not be broadcast because that would flood the querying host with replies.

Two further variants add a third-party capability. Each listed resource carries a qualifier identifying hosts that the confirming host believes may provide the resource. <Who-Anywhere-Provides?> requires a reply if the confirming host knows of any host providing a named resource, and <Does-Anyone-Provide?> requires a reply even if it knows of none. Neither may ever return an IP address that was listed with the resource in the request, which gives a primitive way to exclude known addresses from consideration. These variants let smart hosts supply location information for networks without broadcast capability, and let smart gateways answer for services that are not provided on the local network at all.

Each request type has a reply type. <I-Provide> lists exactly the resources from the request list that the confirming host provides, and <They-Provide> lists those it provides or believes another host provides, each qualified with IP addresses. In both cases the resources must appear in the reply in precisely the order they were listed in the request, and neither reply may be broadcast. A querying host that receives a <They-Provide> reply naming a third host is not required to rely on it unquestioningly; the RFC says the information should usually be treated as a hint, and the host should send a specific <Do-You-Provide?> request to the third host and confirm the resource there first.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to ask. Two ask only about the host that receives the question, and two also allow that host to name other hosts it believes provide the service. Two replies come back: one for what the host itself provides, and one for what it believes others provide.

sections.title: Message Formats and Resource Lists
sections.content:
RLP messages are encapsulated in UDP packets, to take advantage of the multiplexing that the UDP source and destination ports give and the extra reliability that the UDP checksum gives. Requests are sent from a convenient source port on the querying host to the assigned RLP destination port of a receiving host, and replies come back from the assigned RLP source port of the confirming host to the destination port of the querying host, as determined by the source port in the request.

Each RLP packet has a general format of a one-octet Type field, a one-octet Flags field and a two-octet Message-ID, followed by the resource list, which runs to the end of the UDP packet and is therefore sized implicitly by the length of the datagram. The Type field identifies the message type: 0 for <Who-Provides?>, 1 for <Do-You-Provide?>, 2 for <Who-Anywhere-Provides?>, 3 for <Does-Anyone-Provide?>, 4 for <I-Provide> and 5 for <They-Provide>, with 6 to 255 reserved. The Message-ID identifies the request and is simply used to match requests with replies; the receiving host must return the same value in the Message-ID of its reply. Multi-octet quantities are stored from the high-order octet to the low-order octet.

The Flags field carries one defined bit. Bit 1 is <Local-Only>, which requires that any reply may only name IP addresses on the same IP network as the sender of the request, and which requires multi-homed hosts answering broadcast requests to use the appropriate local network source address. This bit must be zero in reply messages, and bits 2 to 8 are reserved and must be zero.

A resource list is a sequence of resource specifiers. Each specifier begins with a Protocol field holding the protocol number of the lowest-level Internet protocol used to access the resource, and an IDLength field giving the length of the identifier that follows. The length may be fixed or variable, and is included so that a specifier naming a resource the host cannot provide can be skipped over without knowing the structure of that identifier. If the protocol has no natural identifier the length is 0 and the identifier field is empty.

In the third-party request and reply types, each resource specifier also carries a qualifier: an IPLength octet followed by an IP address list of four-octet addresses. In a request, IPLength is the maximum number of qualifying addresses the reply may include, and the addresses listed are hosts for which resource information may not be returned; they should normally be initialised to a harmless value such as the querying host's own address. In a reply, IPLength is the number of qualifying addresses known to provide the resource, and it may not exceed the number given in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has four octets of header: what kind of message it is, one flag byte, and a two-byte number so the reply can be matched to the request. After that comes the list of resources being asked about, each one naming a protocol, the length of its identifier, and the identifier itself.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The first scenario has a freshly rebooted host looking for a gateway on its directly connected network to which it can send its first external packet. It broadcasts a <Who-Provides?> request with the Local-Only flag and the resource list [GGP, EGP], which encodes as an eight-octet message. A gateway that understands EGP receives it and returns an <I-Provide> reply with the resource list [EGP], a six-octet message. A second gateway that understands both GGP and EGP may also receive the request, and returns an <I-Provide> reply with the resource list [GGP, EGP].

The second scenario has a host that has hit a fatal software error and wants to find a crash dump server. The crash dump protocol on its local network runs over TFTP, and the special file name CRASH-DUMP marks crash dump processing, so the host broadcasts a <Who-Provides?> request with the resource list [UDP, TFTP, WRQ, "CRASH-DUMP"], a 21-octet message. The file name is explicitly terminated by a null so as not to exclude a future further specialisation of the crash dump protocol. A host that supports this specialisation of TFTP replies with the same resource list. A host that provides plain TFTP but not the specialisation determines that it provides no support, because the name contains components after the UDP port number that it does not understand, and returns no reply at all.

The third scenario has a host on a network without broadcast capability looking for a domain name translation server anywhere on the Internet, and a known resource location server on that network. The querying host first sends a <Does-Anyone-Provide?> request with the Local-Only flag, naming the domain name server port over both TCP and UDP and listing itself as an address to be excluded. The resource location server finds two candidate hosts but neither is on the querying host's network, so it returns a <They-Provide> reply with an empty resource list. The querying host then reissues the request without the Local-Only flag. Because it provided space for only one qualifying address per resource, the server can return only the first candidate, and it does. The querying host then confirms that candidate directly with a <Do-You-Provide?> request, which is denied, and finally asks the resource location server again while excluding the first candidate, which returns the second candidate, and that one confirms that it provides domain name translation on UDP port 53.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same idea in three situations: finding a gateway, finding a crash dump server, and finding a name server on a network that cannot broadcast. In the last case the host has to check the answer for itself rather than trust it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 887 has no security considerations section. The one piece of guidance it gives about trusting what comes back is in the description of reply messages: a querying host that receives a <They-Provide> reply naming a third host is not required to rely on that information unquestioningly. The RFC says the information should usually be regarded simply as a hint, and that in most cases the querying host should transmit a specific <Do-You-Provide?> request to the third host and confirm that the resource really is provided at that IP address before proceeding.

The protocol carries its messages in UDP, which the RFC says is used to gain the multiplexing of the source and destination ports and the extra reliability of the UDP checksum. Nothing in the document addresses who may answer a request, and the Local-Only flag restricts where an answer may point rather than who may send it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about attacks. Its one instruction about trust is that a hint about a third host should be checked directly before you rely on it.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The message type: 0 Who-Provides?, 1 Do-You-Provide?, 2 Who-Anywhere-Provides?, 3 Does-Anyone-Provide?, 4 I-Provide, 5 They-Provide.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 1 is Local-Only, which limits a reply to addresses on the sender's own network. Bits 2 to 8 are reserved and must be zero.

fields.name: Message-ID
fields.desc: Two octets that identify the request, so that the reply can be matched to it.

items.label: Who-Provides?
items.desc: Reply naming the resources provided, but only if the host provides at least one.

items.label: Do-You-Provide?
items.desc: As above, but a reply must always be returned, with an empty list if nothing matches.

items.label: Who-Anywhere-Provides?
items.desc: The third-party variant: reply with the confirming host's own address and those of hosts it believes provide the resource.

items.label: Does-Anyone-Provide?
items.desc: The third-party variant that always replies, even with an empty list.

items.label: I-Provide
items.desc: The reply listing exactly the resources the confirming host provides.

items.label: They-Provide
items.desc: The reply listing resources the confirming host provides or believes another host provides.
